rationale: Ammon rejoices at Israel's devastation and Judah's captivity. Obadiah similarly forbids rejoicing over Judah's destruction or joining the attack on Jerusalem, addressing Idumea rather than Ammon and also forbidding interference with escape routes.
source_text: and say to Ammon’s sons, ‘Hear the Lord’s word! Thus says the Lord: Because you rejoiced over My holy things when they were profaned, over Israel’s land when it was devastated, and over Judah’s house when they went into captivity,

target_units.text: From the day you stood opposed, on the day foreigners took his strength captive and strangers entered his gates and cast lots over Jerusalem, you too were like one of them.

relationship: related profanation of holy places accompanied by neighbors' scorn
rationale: Ammon's offense includes rejoicing when God's holy things were profaned. The psalm describes nations defiling God's temple and Jerusalem's ruin, followed by neighbors' sneering and ridicule, supplying the particular sacred-place and hostile-response combination.
source_text: and say to Ammon’s sons, ‘Hear the Lord’s word! Thus says the Lord: Because you rejoiced over My holy things when they were profaned, over Israel’s land when it was devastated, and over Judah’s house when they went into captivity,

They poured out their blood like water around Jerusalem, and there was no one to bury them.

relationship: same-chapter repeated grant to Kedem's sons
rationale: God gives Ammon to Kedem's sons as an inheritance, with their camps and consumption of its produce. Verse 10 repeats the grant to Kedem's sons against Ammon and adds the end of Ammon's remembrance; it does not repeat the food details.
source_text: therefore behold, I am handing you to the sons of Kedem as an inheritance. They will camp with their equipment in you and set their dwellings in you. They will eat your fruits and drink your richness.

target_units.text: To Kedem’s sons, against Ammon’s sons, I have given them as an inheritance, so that no remembrance of Ammon’s sons may remain.

relationship: related conversion of inhabited territory into animal pasture
rationale: Ammon's city becomes camel pasture and Ammon's sons a pasture for sheep. Zephaniah likewise describes Crete becoming pasture and sheep enclosure, with grazing in Ashkelon's houses; the territory differs and the target does not mention camels.
source_text: I will make Ammon’s city pastures for camels, and Ammon’s sons a pasture for sheep. You will recognize that I am the Lord.

target_units.text: Crete will become pasture for flocks and an enclosure for sheep,

and the seacoast will belong to the remnant of Judah’s house. They will graze upon them in Ashkelon’s houses; at evening they will lodge away from the sons of Judah, for the Lord their God has visited them and turned their captivity.

relationship: parallel clapping and hostile rejoicing over Israel's calamity
rationale: Ammon claps, makes noise with the foot and rejoices over Israel's land. Lamentations likewise reports passersby clapping at Jerusalem and enemies rejoicing over her downfall, without repeating Ezekiel's foot gesture.
source_text: For thus says the Lord: Because you clapped your hand and made noise with your foot, and rejoiced from your soul over Israel’s land,

target_units.text: All who pass along the road clapped their hands at you. They hissed and shook their heads at Daughter Jerusalem: “Is this the city they will call a crown of glory, the gladness of all the earth?”
All your enemies opened their mouths against you. They hissed and gnashed their teeth; they said, “We have swallowed her! Indeed, this is the day we expected; we found it, we saw it!”
The Lord did what He intended; He fulfilled His words, which He commanded from ancient days. He brought down without sparing; He made the enemy rejoice over you and exalted your oppressor’s horn.

relationship: parallel plunder of Ammon following hostility to God's people
rationale: Ezekiel threatens Ammon with plunder among nations and destruction after its rejoicing over Israel. Zephaniah also names Ammon's hostility and promises plunder and inheritance, there specifically by the remnant of God's people.
source_text: therefore I will stretch My hand against you, give you to plunder among the nations, utterly destroy you from the peoples and make you perish from the countries with destruction. You will recognize that I am the Lord.’

target_units.text: I heard Moab’s reproaches and the Ammonites’ blows, with which they reproached My people and exalted themselves against My borders.

Therefore, as I live, says the Lord of powers, the God of Israel, Moab will be like Sodom and the Ammonites like Gomorrah, and Damascus abandoned like a heap on a threshing floor and vanished forever. My people’s remnant will plunder them; My nation’s remnant will inherit them.
This will be theirs for their arrogance, because they reproached and exalted themselves against the Lord Almighty.

relationship: contrast with the claim that Israel is merely like other nations
rationale: Moab dismisses Israel and Judah as like all nations. Deuteronomy instead distinguishes Israel before the nations through its wisdom, God's nearness and its righteous laws, supplying a specific contrast to that dismissal rather than a prediction of Moab's punishment.
source_text: Thus says the Lord: Because Moab said, ‘Behold, Israel’s and Judah’s house is like all the nations,’

target_units.text: And you shall keep and do them; for this is your wisdom and understanding before all the nations, who shall hear all these ordinances and say: Behold, this great nation is a wise and understanding people.
For what great nation is there whose god draws near unto them, as the Lord our God in all things wherein we call upon Him?
And what great nation is there that has ordinances and judgments as righteous as all this law which I set before you this day?

relationship: repeated Ammon oracle ending with no remembrance
rationale: Ezekiel 25 ends the grant against Ammon with the loss of its remembrance. The earlier oracle explicitly names Ammon and likewise ends with no remembrance after judgment in its land, while describing fire and blood rather than the grant to Kedem.

and pour My anger upon you. I will blow upon you with the fire of My anger and hand you into the hands of barbarian men devising destruction.

relationship: parallel divine judgment upon Moab with different stated offenses
rationale: Ezekiel announces vengeance upon Moab following its dismissive statement about Israel and Judah. Amos likewise announces Moab's judgment, there for burning Idumea's king's bones and with the destruction of rulers; the charges and particular penalties differ.
source_text: I will exact vengeance upon Moab, and they will recognize that I am the Lord.

target_units.text: Thus says the Lord: “For three impieties of Moab, and for four, I will not turn away from him, because they burned the bones of Idumea’s king into lime.
I will send fire upon Moab, and it will devour the foundations of her cities. Moab will die in weakness, with shouting and the sound of a trumpet.
I will destroy the judge from her, and kill all her rulers with him,” says the Lord.

relationship: parallel indictment of Idumea for violence toward Judah
rationale: Idumea's vengeance and grudge against Judah provoke judgment. Obadiah likewise condemns Idumea's slaughter and impiety toward brother Jacob, then identifies Jerusalem and Judah's disaster and forbids harm to fugitives.
source_text: Thus says the Lord: Because Idumea acted in vengeance against Judah’s house, and they bore a grudge and exacted punishment,

target_units.text: because of the slaughter and the impiety toward your brother Jacob; and shame will cover you, and you will be removed forever.

Do not stand at their escape routes to destroy those of them who are being saved, and do not shut in those fleeing from them on the day of affliction.

relationship: parallel desolation of Idumea and its named region
rationale: Ezekiel threatens Idumea with wilderness and sword, naming those pursued from Thaiman. Jeremiah likewise announces uninhabitable Idumea and a destructive purpose against Teman's inhabitants, preserving the different name forms and the target's own images.
source_text: therefore thus says the Lord: I will stretch My hand against Idumea and utterly destroy human and animal from her. I will make her a wilderness, and those pursued from Thaiman will fall by the sword.

target_units.text: Idumea will become an untrodden place; everyone passing by her will hiss.
As Sodom, Gomorrah, and her neighboring places were overturned, said the Lord Almighty, no person will settle there, and no human being will live there.

Like a lion he will come up from Jordan’s midst into Aitham’s place, for I will quickly drive them away from her. Appoint the young men over her. For who is like Me? Who will resist Me, and what shepherd can stand before Me?

Therefore hear the Lord’s counsel that He planned against Idumea and His purpose against Teman’s inhabitants: Surely the smallest sheep will be swept together; surely their dwelling will be made untrodden over her.

relationship: parallel judgment of Esau's land through Israel's people
rationale: Ezekiel makes God's people Israel the instrument of vengeance upon Idumea. Obadiah depicts Jacob and Joseph consuming Esau like fire and men from Zion executing judgment upon Esau's mountain, connecting the divine judgment with those named human agents.
source_text: I will place My vengeance upon Idumea by the hand of My people Israel. They will act in Idumea according to My anger and My wrath, and they will recognize My vengeance, says the Lord.

target_units.text: The house of Jacob will be a fire, the house of Joseph a flame, and the house of Esau stubble. They will blaze against them and consume them, and there will be no bearer of fire in the house of Esau, because the Lord has spoken.

Those in the Negeb will possess the mountain of Esau, and those in the Shephelah will possess the foreigners. They will possess the mountain of Ephraim, the plain of Samaria, Benjamin and the land of Gilead.

And this is the beginning of the deportation: for the sons of Israel, the land of the Canaanites as far as Zarephath; and the deportation of Jerusalem as far as Ephrathah. They will inherit the cities of the Negeb.
And men who have been saved shall ascend from Mount Zion to execute judgment upon the mountain of Esau; and the kingdom shall be the Lord’s.

relationship: same-chapter human vengeance answered by divine vengeance
rationale: The foreigners' vengeance and rejoicing in destruction form the charge. The following therefore introduces God's action against the coastal inhabitants and His great vengeance, making the repetition a stated retributive answer rather than identifying an unstated victim in this unit.
source_text: Therefore thus says the Lord: Because the foreigners acted in vengeance and stirred up vengeance, rejoicing from their soul to wipe out for ever,

target_units.text: therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I will stretch My hand against the foreigners, utterly destroy Cretans and make the remaining inhabitants of the coast perish.

relationship: parallel judgment of Cretans and coastal inhabitants
rationale: Ezekiel names Cretans and the remaining inhabitants of the coast in the announced destruction. Zephaniah likewise addresses the seacoast's inhabitants and sojourners of Cretans, threatening destruction and then depicting Crete as pasture; the shared names are retained as supplied.
source_text: therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I will stretch My hand against the foreigners, utterly destroy Cretans and make the remaining inhabitants of the coast perish.

target_units.text: Woe to the seacoast’s inhabitants, sojourners of Cretans! The Lord’s word is against you, Canaan, land of foreigners: I will destroy you from your dwelling.
Crete will become pasture for flocks and an enclosure for sheep,

relationship: same-chapter divine vengeance answering the foreigners' vengeance
rationale: The announced great vengeance concludes the indictment of foreigners who themselves acted in vengeance. Verses 15–16 supply that charge and the therefore introducing God's response, identifying the people addressed by this unit's them.
source_text: I will execute great acts of vengeance upon them. They will recognize that I am the Lord when I bring My vengeance upon them.”

relationship: parallel neighboring nations rejoicing at Judah's downfall
rationale: Tyre greets Jerusalem's shattering with approval and speaks of the full one's devastation. The preceding Ammon oracle likewise condemns rejoicing over profaned holy things, Israel's devastation and Judah's captivity, with different words for the neighboring nation's response.

rationale: God brings many nations against Tyre as the sea rises with its waves. Isaiah likewise compares many nations with a surging sea and abundant rushing water, without identifying Tyre as the target of its own comparison.
source_text: therefore thus says the Lord: I am against you, Tyre, and I will bring many nations against you, as the sea rises with its waves.

target_units.text: Woe, the multitude of many nations! Like a surging sea, so you will be troubled, and the back of many nations will roar like water.

Many nations are like abundant water, like much water violently rushing down. He will drive him away and pursue him far off, like chaff-dust when people winnow before wind, and like wheel-dust carried by a squall.

relationship: same-chapter repeated reduction of Tyre to smooth rock
rationale: The removal of Tyre's walls, towers and dust ends with smooth rock. Verse 14 repeats that smooth-rock outcome and adds a net-drying place and the refusal of rebuilding, developing the city's predicted stripped condition.
source_text: They will throw down Tyre’s walls and throw down your towers. I will winnow her dust from her and make her a smooth rock.

relationship: contrasting net-drying places in ruin and restored life
rationale: Tyre becomes a drying place for nets and plunder in the sea. Ezekiel 47 also names a drying place for nets, there amid healed waters and abundant living fish; the repeated fishing image has a different surrounding purpose.
source_text: She will be a drying place for nets in the midst of the sea, for I have spoken, says the Lord. She will become plunder for the nations,

target_units.text: Every life among the swarming living creatures will live wherever the river comes. There will be very many fish there, because this water has arrived there, and it will become healthy and live. Everything over which the river comes will live.
Fishers will stand there from Aingadin to Ainagalim; there will be a drying place for nets. It will be by itself, and its fish will be like the fish of the Great Sea, an exceedingly great multitude.

relationship: same-chapter repeated sword judgment upon Tyre's daughters in the plain
rationale: Both units predict the killing of Tyre's daughters in the plain by the sword. Verse 8 places that action within the king's campaign and siege works, making the agency more concrete than the earlier announcement.

relationship: shared king-of-kings title for Babylon's ruler
rationale: Ezekiel identifies Nebuchadnezzar as king of Babylon and king of kings. Daniel's interpretation likewise addresses the king as king of kings and attributes his authority to the Lord of heaven, rather than describing the attack on Tyre.

You, O king, are king of kings, and the Lord of heaven has given you rule, kingdom, strength, honor, and glory.
Throughout the inhabited world He has handed over into your hands human beings, wild beasts, birds of heaven, and fish of the sea, to rule them all. You are the golden head.

relationship: later report of Nebuchadnezzar's force serving against Tyre
rationale: Ezekiel 26 announces Nebuchadnezzar's force coming against Tyre. Ezekiel 29 explicitly reports his force's great servitude against Tyre and its lack of wages, supporting the named campaign without asserting an outcome beyond that report.
source_text: For thus says the Lord: I am bringing against you, Tyre, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon from the north—he is king of kings—with horses, chariots, horsemen, and an assembly of very many nations.

target_units.text: “Son of man, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon subjected his force to great servitude against Tyre; every head was bald and every shoulder was losing its hair. Yet neither he nor his force received wages for Tyre and the servitude they performed against her.

rationale: The campaign against Tyre includes building around it and making a palisade and a ring of weapons. source_text: He will kill your daughters in the plain with the sword, set an advance guard against you, build around you, and make a palisade and a ring of weapons around you; he will set his spears opposite you.

The city remained under siege until King Sedekias’s eleventh year.

relationship: same-chapter repeated destruction of walls and towers
rationale: The king will throw down Tyre's walls and towers with his swords. Verse 4 had announced the fall of those same structures under the coming nations, linking the specific agent and weapon with the preceding prediction.
source_text: He will throw down your walls and your towers with his swords.

target_units.text: They will throw down Tyre’s walls and throw down your towers. I will winnow her dust from her and make her a smooth rock.

relationship: parallel horse noise accompanied by shaking
rationale: Tyre's walls shake at the sound of horsemen and chariot wheels as the force enters. Jeremiah likewise describes the sound of horses and the earth shaking at their neighing, retaining the different sound details and scale of the shaking.
source_text: The dust of his multitude of horses will cover you, and your walls will shake at the sound of his horsemen and his chariots’ wheels when he enters your gates like someone entering a city from the plain.

relationship: parallel mounted assault and sword slaughter in a city

rationale: The destruction includes walls and houses, with stones, timber and dust thrown into the sea. Verse 4 had promised broken walls and towers and the removal of Tyre's dust; the later detail adds the debris and its destination.
source_text: He will plunder your strength, strip your possessions, throw down your walls, and demolish your desirable houses. He will throw your stones, timber, and dust into the sea.

target_units.text: They will throw down Tyre’s walls and throw down your towers. I will winnow her dust from her and make her a smooth rock.

relationship: parallel cessation of music in judgment
rationale: Tyre's musicians are brought to an end and its psalteries are no longer heard. Isaiah likewise announces ceased tambourine joy and a ceased lyre sound, preserving the named instruments rather than making every instrument identical.
source_text: He will put an end to the multitude of your musicians, and the sound of your psalteries will certainly no longer be heard.

target_units.text: The joy of tambourines has ceased; the impudence and wealth of the ungodly have ceased; the lyre’s sound has ceased.

relationship: same-chapter combination of smooth rock and net-drying place
rationale: The smooth rock and drying place for nets repeat the two earlier descriptions of stripped Tyre. This unit brings them together and adds that the city will not be rebuilt, an additional statement not supplied by the earlier pair alone.
source_text: I will make you a smooth rock, a drying place for nets. You will certainly not be rebuilt, for I have spoken, says the Lord.

target_units.text: They will throw down Tyre’s walls and throw down your towers. I will winnow her dust from her and make her a smooth rock.

relationship: contrast between Tyre not rebuilt and Tyre restored
rationale: Ezekiel declares that Tyre will certainly not be rebuilt. Isaiah's Tyre oracle instead describes restoration to its former state after seventy years and renewed trade; the differing prophetic statements are preserved without inventing a harmonizing timetable.
source_text: I will make you a smooth rock, a drying place for nets. You will certainly not be rebuilt, for I have spoken, says the Lord.

target_units.text: On that day Tyre will be left for seventy years, like a king’s time, like a person’s time. After seventy years, Tyre will be like a prostitute’s song:
“Take a lyre, wander through cities, forgotten prostitute! Play the lyre well, sing much, so that you may be remembered.”
After seventy years God will visit Tyre, and she will again be restored to her former state and become a trading center for all the inhabited world’s kingdoms.

relationship: related island response to Tyre's fall
rationale: Ezekiel 26 asks whether the islands will shake at Tyre's fall amid groaning and the sword. Ezekiel 27 likewise portrays the island inhabitants becoming gloomy and their kings astonished and tearful, describing further reactions to the same city's downfall.
source_text: For thus says the Lord, the Lord, to Tyre: Will not the islands shake at the sound of your fall, when the wounded groan and a sword is drawn within you?

target_units.text: All who inhabit the islands became gloomy over you; their kings were utterly astonished, and their faces shed tears.

relationship: related royal departure from throne and changed dress in crisis
rationale: Sea-nation rulers step down from thrones, remove headwear and patterned clothes, and sit on the ground in fear over Tyre. Nineveh's king likewise rises from his throne, removes his robe and sits in ashes wearing sackcloth, there in response to Jonah's warning and as part of repentance.
source_text: All the rulers from the nations of the sea will step down from their thrones, remove the turbans from their heads, and strip off their patterned clothing. They will be utterly astonished, sit on the ground, fear their own destruction, and groan over you.

target_units.text: The word reached the king of Nineveh. He rose from his throne, took his robe off himself, wrapped himself in sackcloth and sat in ashes.

relationship: parallel lament over Tyre's maritime prominence
rationale: The sea rulers raise a lament over Tyre as a praised city destroyed from the sea. Ezekiel 27 likewise commands a lament for Tyre and describes its place at the sea's entrance and its trade with many islands, preserving the different lamenting voices.
source_text: They will raise a lament over you and say to you: ‘How you were destroyed from the sea, praised city that spread her fear to all who live in her!

relationship: related distress among maritime neighbors over Tyre
rationale: Ezekiel predicts the islands' fear from the day Tyre falls. Isaiah's Tyre oracle likewise describes pain reaching Egypt and orders island residents to wail, with different emotions and named surrounding places.
source_text: The islands will be afraid from the day of your fall.’

target_units.text: When it becomes known to Egypt, pain will seize them concerning Tyre.
Go away to Carthage! Wail, residents of this island!

relationship: shared sea covering and uninhabitable city imagery
rationale: Tyre becomes uninhabited as the abyss and much water cover it. Jeremiah likewise depicts the sea rising over Babylon and covering her, followed by cities without inhabitants; the different cities and Jeremiah's ensuing waterless-land image remain distinct.
source_text: For thus says the Lord, the Lord: When I make you a desolated city like cities that will not be inhabited, when I bring the abyss up over you and much water covers you,

target_units.text: The sea rose over Babylon with the sound of its waves, and she was covered.
Her cities became a waterless and untrodden land; not one person will live there, nor will any human lodge there.

relationship: related descent among the ancient dead
rationale: Tyre is brought down among people of old in the earth's depths and those descending to a pit. Isaiah likewise portrays Babylon's king meeting prior earthly rulers in Hades and descending to the earth's foundations; the city and royal figure are different subjects of the descent imagery.
source_text: I will bring you down to those descending into the pit, to the people of old. I will settle you in the depths of the earth like an everlasting wilderness, with those descending into the pit, so that you are not inhabited and do not rise in the land of life.

target_units.text: Hades below grew bitter on meeting you. All the giants who ruled the earth rose together for you, those who raised all the nations’ kings from their thrones.
They will all answer and say to you, ‘You too were captured as we were, and were numbered among us.’
Your glory went down to Hades, your abundant gladness. They will spread decay beneath you, and your covering is a worm.
How the dawn-bearer who rises in the morning fell from heaven! The one dispatching to all the nations was shattered to earth.
You said in your mind, ‘I will ascend to heaven, set my throne above heaven’s stars, and sit on a high mountain, upon the high mountains toward the north.
I will ascend above the clouds; I will be like the Most High.’
But now you will descend to Hades and to the earth’s foundations.

relationship: repeated permanent-ruin refrain for Tyre
rationale: Ezekiel 26 ends by announcing Tyre's ruin and that it will no longer exist for ever. The following Tyre lament ends with the same ruin-and-no-more refrain, there also reporting the traders' hissing.
source_text: I will bring you to ruin, and you will no longer exist for ever, says the Lord, the Lord.”

target_units.text: Traders from nations hissed at you; you came to ruin, and you will be no more for ever.’”

relationship: repeated lament directed toward Tyre
rationale: Ezekiel is commanded to take up a lament for Tyre. The preceding oracle depicts sea rulers raising a lament over the same city, identifying both the shared genre and the different voices who deliver it.
source_text: “Son of man, take up a lament over Tyre,

relationship: related beauty of Tyre and adornment of its ruler
rationale: Tyre says it clothed itself with beauty. The lament over its ruler calls him a crown of beauty and enumerates his precious stones, transferring the beauty motif to a royal addressee without making every detail of city and ruler identical.
source_text: and say to Tyre, who dwells at the entrance of the sea, the trading place of the peoples from many islands: Thus says the Lord to Tyre: You said, ‘I have clothed myself with my beauty.’

you came to be in the delight of God’s paradise. relationship: same-chapter repeated clothing with beauty
rationale: The account of Tyre's place at Beelim and in the sea says its sons clothed it with beauty. The preceding unit has Tyre itself say that it clothed itself with beauty, retaining the different stated agents of the repeated image.
source_text: In the heart of the sea, at Beelim, your sons clothed you with beauty.

target_units.text: and say to Tyre, who dwells at the entrance of the sea, the trading place of the peoples from many islands: Thus says the Lord to Tyre: You said, ‘I have clothed myself with my beauty.’

relationship: related Tyrian use of Lebanon timber with maritime handling
rationale: Tyre's materials include cypress from Lebanon for its masts. Hiram of Tyre supplies cedar and pine timber brought from Lebanon to the sea as rafts; the comparison concerns Tyrian access to Lebanon timber and its maritime use, preserving the different timber descriptions.
source_text: Cedar from Senir was built for you; strips of cypress planks were taken from Lebanon to make fir masts for you.

target_units.text: Now command that they cut timber from Lebanon for me. Behold, my servants are with your servants, and I will pay you the wages of your service according to whatever you say; for you know that no one among us knows how to cut timber like the Sidonians.”
When Hiram heard Solomon’s words, he rejoiced greatly and said, “Blessed be God this day, who has given David a discerning son over this great people!”
He sent to Solomon, saying, “I have heard about everything you did send to me. I will fulfill all your wishes: cedar and pine timber.

My servants will bring them down from Lebanon to the sea. I will make them into rafts as far as the place you send me word about, and shake them apart there; you shall take them away. You shall fulfill my wish by providing loaves for my household.”
Hiram supplied Solomon with cedars and all that he desired.

relationship: related ivory structures within judgment upon costly buildings
rationale: Ezekiel names Tyre's sacred places of ivory and wooded houses from Kittim's islands. Amos likewise mentions ivory houses that will perish amid judgment on Israel's buildings; the material and vulnerable structures correspond, while their stated sacred or domestic character differs.
source_text: From Bashan they made your oars; they made your sacred places from ivory, wooded houses from the islands of Kittim.

target_units.text: “Hear and bear witness to Jacob’s house,” says the Lord God Almighty,
“because on the day I exact judgment upon Israel for its impieties, I will also exact judgment upon Bethel’s altars. The altar’s horns will be demolished and fall upon the ground,
and I will confound and strike the colonnaded house along with the summer house. Ivory houses will perish, and many other houses will be added,” says the Lord.

relationship: shared Egyptian textiles furnishing a bed
rationale: Tyre's bedding is embroidered fine linen from Egypt. The woman in Proverbs likewise describes Egyptian textiles spread on her bed, there double-sided rugs; the shared origin and furnishing use do not make the fabrics or narrative settings identical.
source_text: Fine linen with embroidery from Egypt became your bedding, to clothe you with glory and wrap you in blue and purple from the islands of Elishah; it became your coverings.

target_units.text: I have stretched my bed with bands and spread it with double-sided rugs from Egypt.

relationship: same-chapter rowers and pilots in service and calamity
rationale: The maritime portrait names Tyre's rowers and wise pilots. Later their occupational groups recur as pilots become afraid and rowers leave ships, contrasting the earlier organized service with the lament's response to disaster without identifying every later rower individually.
source_text: Your rulers who inhabit Sidon, and the Arvadites, became your rowers; your wise men, Tyre, who were in you, were your pilots.

target_units.text: At the sound of your cry, your pilots will be greatly afraid,
and all your rowers will come down from the ships; the passengers and the lookouts of the sea will stand on the land.

relationship: same-chapter counselors included in Tyre's loss
rationale: Byblos's elders and wise people strengthen Tyre's counsel. The catastrophe later includes counselors among the people and resources falling in the sea; the shared role does not identify every later counselor as a member of the earlier Byblos group.
source_text: The elders of Byblos and their wise men were in you; they strengthened your counsel. All the ships of the sea and their rowers came to you toward the farthest west.

target_units.text: There were your forces, your payment and that of your mixed companies, your rowers and pilots, your counselors and your mixed companies from your mixed companies, all your warrior men in you, and your whole assembly within you; they will fall in the heart of the sea on the day of your fall.

relationship: overlapping named foreign peoples in military judgment lists
rationale: Persians, Lydians and Libyans appear in Tyre's force, with shields and helmets contributing to its glory. The Egypt oracle also names these three peoples among those falling by the sword, with additional peoples and without repeating all the equipment.
source_text: Persians, Lydians, and Libyans were in your force; your warrior men hung small shields and helmets in you; they gave you your glory.

target_units.text: Persians, Cretans, Lydians, Libyans, all the mixed company, and some of the sons of My covenant will fall by the sword in her.

relationship: contrast between Tyre's guarded fortifications and their destruction
rationale: Sons of Arvadites are on Tyre's walls and guards in its towers, with quivers around its harbors. The preceding oracle predicts destruction of those walls and towers; the shared structures connect the display of defense with their announced fall.
source_text: Sons of Arvadites and your force were on your walls; guards were in your towers. They hung their quivers around your harbors; they completed your beauty.

target_units.text: They will throw down Tyre’s walls and throw down your towers. I will winnow her dust from her and make her a smooth rock.

relationship: related Carthaginian commerce in Tyre's rise and loss
rationale: Carthaginians are named as Tyre's trading partners in metals. Isaiah's Tyre oracle instead announces that ships no longer come from Carthage, connecting the named commercial relationship with its cessation without importing that oracle's statement into Ezekiel's metal list.
source_text: Carthaginians were your traders because of the abundance of all your strength; they gave silver, gold, iron, tin, and lead for your market.

target_units.text: Work your land, for ships no longer come from Carthage.

relationship: related trade in human lives involving Tyre and Greeks
rationale: Ezekiel names Greece and adjoining places in Tyre's trade in human lives and bronze. Joel directly addresses Tyre and Sidon for selling Judah's and Jerusalem's sons to Greeks; the particular human commerce is shared, while Joel specifies victims and the direction of sale.
source_text: Greece, all of it, and the adjoining regions traded with you in human lives, and gave bronze vessels for your commerce.

target_units.text: What have you to do with Me, Tyre and Sidon and all Galilee of foreigners? Are you repaying Me a recompense? Or do you bear a sharp grudge against Me? I will speedily repay your recompense upon your heads,
because you took My silver and gold and brought My chosen and beautiful things into your temples,
and sold the sons of Judah and the sons of Jerusalem to the sons of the Greeks, so as to thrust them out of their own borders.

relationship: parallel international horse trade
rationale: Horses and horsemen from the house of Togarmah are given for Tyre's market. Kings likewise describes horses from Egypt and Thekoue, merchants obtaining them from Thekoue, and Egyptian export prices for Hittite and Syrian royal recipients. The particular horse trade corresponds without equating the partners or adding horsemen to the target's goods.
source_text: From the house of Togarmah they gave horses and horsemen for your market.

target_units.text: Solomon’s horses came from Egypt and from Thekoue; the king’s merchants obtained them from Thekoue in exchange.
The export from Egypt came up: a chariot for a hundred pieces of silver, and a horse for fifty pieces of silver. In this way they went out by sea for all the Hittite kings and the kings of Syria.

relationship: related wheat and oil supplied to Tyre from Israel
rationale: Judah and Israel trade grain and oil among other goods with Tyre. Kings describes Solomon supplying Hiram with wheat and beaten oil each year within their covenant relationship, providing a concrete counterpart for those two goods rather than all items in Ezekiel's catalog.
source_text: Judah and the sons of Israel were your traders in the sale of grain, perfumes, and cassia; they gave choice honey, oil, and resin to your mixed company.

target_units.text: Solomon gave Hiram twenty thousand kors of wheat and machir for his household, and twenty thousand beth of beaten oil. Solomon gave this to Hiram each year.
The Lord gave Solomon wisdom, as He had promised him. There was peace between Hiram and Solomon, and they made a covenant between themselves.

relationship: related Kedar livestock directed to different destinations
rationale: Ezekiel lists Arabia and Kedar in trade involving camels, rams and lambs. Isaiah likewise brings Kedar's sheep, alongside Nabaioth's rams, to the restored addressee and God's altar; the named livestock connection is shared while trade and acceptable offering differ.
source_text: Arabia and all the rulers of Kedar were your traders through your hand, with camels, rams, and lambs in which they traded with you.

target_units.text: herds of camels, and camels from Madiam and Gaipha will cover you. They will all come from Saba, bringing gold and carrying frankincense, and they will proclaim the Lord’s salvation as good news.
All Kedar’s sheep will gather to you, and Nabaioth’s rams will come to you. They will be offered acceptably upon My altar, and My house of prayer will be glorified.

relationship: shared Sheba association with spices, precious stones and gold
rationale: Sheba and Raamah trade spices, good stones and gold with Tyre. Kings likewise names Sheba's queen giving Solomon spices, precious stones and gold, matching the three goods while distinguishing a royal gift from Tyre's commerce.
source_text: Traders of Sheba and Raamah were your traders with choice spices and good stones, and they gave gold for your market.

target_units.text: She gave Solomon a hundred twenty talents of gold, very many spices, and precious stones. Never again came such an abundance of spices as the queen of Sheba gave King Solomon.

relationship: related Carthaginian ships in Tyre's commerce and downfall
rationale: The continuation mentioning ships names Carthaginian trade and Tyre's abundance in the sea. Isaiah addresses ships of Carthage with a command to wail because their fortress has perished, connecting that shipping world with Tyre's loss rather than repeating the full cargo list.
source_text: ships: in them Carthaginians were your traders in abundance among your mixed company. You were filled and became very heavy in the heart of the sea.

target_units.text: Wail, ships of Carthage, because your fortress has perished!

relationship: shared wind shattering ships
rationale: A south wind shatters Tyre in the heart of the sea within the ship portrait. The psalm likewise speaks of a violent wind shattering Tarshish's ships; it supplies no compass direction and should not be used to replace Ezekiel's south wind.
source_text: Your rowers led you in much water; the south wind shattered you in the heart of the sea.

target_units.text: With a violent wind Thou wilt shatter the ships of Tarshish.

relationship: same-chapter repeated loss of assembly and crew in the sea
rationale: Tyre's forces, payments, crews, counselors and assembly fall in the sea on the day of its fall. Verse 34 repeats the shattering in the sea's depth and the fall of the mixed company, assembly and rowers, concentrating the same collective loss.
source_text: There were your forces, your payment and that of your mixed companies, your rowers and pilots, your counselors and your mixed companies from your mixed companies, all your warrior men in you, and your whole assembly within you; they will fall in the heart of the sea on the day of your fall.

target_units.text: Now you were shattered in the sea, in the depth of water; your mixed company and all your assembly fell within you—all your rowers.

relationship: related sound and fear at Tyre's downfall
rationale: The sound of crying frightens the pilots in this lament. The preceding Tyre oracle likewise links the sound of the city's fall and wounded people's groans with the islands' shaking, preserving the different frightened groups and sounds.
source_text: At the sound of your cry, your pilots will be greatly afraid,

target_units.text: For thus says the Lord, the Lord, to Tyre: Will not the islands shake at the sound of your fall, when the wounded groan and a sword is drawn within you?

relationship: same-chapter rowers in Tyre's maritime portrait and lament
rationale: All the rowers leave the ships as passengers and lookouts stand on land. Verse 8 had named rulers inhabiting Sidon and the Arvadites as rowers serving Tyre; the repeated occupation links the maritime service with the later response without asserting that every person in the two groups is identical.
source_text: and all your rowers will come down from the ships; the passengers and the lookouts of the sea will stand on the land.

target_units.text: Your rulers who inhabit Sidon, and the Arvadites, became your rowers; your wise men, Tyre, who were in you, were your pilots.

relationship: shared dust-on-head gesture after communal calamity
rationale: Those mourning Tyre put earth on their heads and spread ashes beneath them. Joshua and Israel's elders likewise put dust on their heads after the loss at Ai, matching the head gesture while preserving the different disasters and Ezekiel's additional ashes.
source_text: They will raise a cry over you with their voice and cry bitterly; they will put earth on their head and spread ashes beneath them.

target_units.text: The men of Ai killed about thirty-six of them, pursued them from the gate, and crushed them on the descent. The people’s heart was terrified and became like water.
Joshua tore his clothes and fell face down on the earth before the Lord until evening, he and the elders of Israel. They put dust on their heads.

And Joshua said, “I beseech Thee, Lord, why did Thy servant bring this people across the Jordan, to deliver them to the Amorites and destroy us? Would that we had remained and dwelt beside the Jordan!
What can I say, since Israel has turned its back before its enemy?
When the Canaanites and all the inhabitants of the land hear, they shall surround us and blot us out from the earth. And what wilt Thou do for Thy great name?”

relationship: repeated lament over Tyre's destruction
rationale: The sons raise a lament for Tyre, whose destruction in the sea is described in the following units. The preceding oracle likewise gives a lament over the praised maritime city, there raised by sea rulers; the subject and loss recur with different lamenting groups.
source_text: Their sons will take up a lament over you and a lamentation for you:

target_units.text: They will raise a lament over you and say to you: ‘How you were destroyed from the sea, praised city that spread her fear to all who live in her!

relationship: related Tyrian commerce and royal prominence
rationale: Tyre finds payment from the sea, fills nations from its abundance and enriches kings from its mixed company. Isaiah likewise portrays Tyre's merchants as glorious rulers of the earth before announcing their humiliation; it emphasizes status rather than repeating Ezekiel's specific statement that Tyre enriched kings.
source_text: ‘What a payment you found from the sea! You filled nations from your abundance, and from your mixed company you enriched all the kings of the earth.

target_units.text: Who planned these things against Tyre? Is she weaker, or has she no strength? Her merchants are glorious, rulers of the earth.
The Lord Sabaoth planned it, to dissolve all the insolence of the glorious and dishonor everything glorious upon the earth.

relationship: same-chapter repeated sinking of Tyre's company and rowers
rationale: The city's shattering in deep water brings its mixed company, assembly and rowers down. Verse 27 had already gathered the force, payments and crews into a collective fall in the sea, making the later line a specific repetition of their shared loss.
source_text: Now you were shattered in the sea, in the depth of water; your mixed company and all your assembly fell within you—all your rowers.

target_units.text: There were your forces, your payment and that of your mixed companies, your rowers and pilots, your counselors and your mixed companies from your mixed companies, all your warrior men in you, and your whole assembly within you; they will fall in the heart of the sea on the day of your fall.

relationship: repeated island response to Tyre's fall
rationale: Island inhabitants become gloomy, and their kings are astonished with tears on their faces. The preceding oracle had announced the islands' fear from Tyre's fall; the shared island audience is retained while the later lament adds particular reactions.
source_text: All who inhabit the islands became gloomy over you; their kings were utterly astonished, and their faces shed tears.

target_units.text: The islands will be afraid from the day of your fall.’

relationship: repeated permanent-ruin refrain for Tyre
rationale: The lament ends with traders hissing and Tyre becoming ruin and no longer existing for ever. Ezekiel 26 had ended with the same ruin-and-no-more declaration, supplying the particular repeated conclusion rather than merely a general judgment theme.
source_text: Traders from nations hissed at you; you came to ruin, and you will be no more for ever.’”

target_units.text: I will bring you to ruin, and you will no longer exist for ever, says the Lord, the Lord.”

relationship: related divine claims and occupation of a purported divine place
rationale: Tyre's ruler claims to be a god and to occupy a god's dwelling in the sea, although he is human. The man of lawlessness likewise takes a seat in God's sanctuary displaying himself as God; the comparison concerns the divine claims and occupation of a divine place, without identifying the figures or locations as the same.
source_text: “And you, son of man, say to the ruler of Tyre: Thus says the Lord: Because your heart was exalted and you said, ‘I am a god; I have inhabited a god’s dwelling in the heart of the sea’—yet you are a human, and not a god, and you made your heart like a god’s heart—

target_units.text: Let no one deceive you in any way. For that day will not come unless the rebellion comes first and the man of lawlessness is revealed, the son of destruction,
who opposes and exalts himself above everything called god or an object of worship, so that he takes his seat in God’s sanctuary, displaying himself as being God.

relationship: Daniel's divine disclosure beside the challenge to Tyre's wisdom
rationale: The ruler is challenged with the question whether he is wiser than Daniel. Daniel describes God as the revealer of mysteries and expressly denies that the disclosure came through wisdom exceeding all people, illuminating the named comparison without adding a secrets-hidden clause to Ezekiel.
source_text: Surely you are not wiser than Daniel? Did wise men not instruct you in their knowledge?

target_units.text: Daniel spoke aloud before the king, “Disclosure of the mystery the king saw does not belong to wise men, sorcerers, incantation-singers, or gazarenes,

but there is a God in heaven who uncovers mysteries, who has disclosed to King Nebuchadnezzar what must happen in the last days. O king, live for ever! This is the dream and the vision of your head upon your bed:
You, O king, reclining upon your bed, saw everything that must happen in the last days, and the Revealer of mysteries disclosed to you what must happen.
This mystery was revealed to me because of no wisdom in me beyond all people; rather, so that it might be disclosed to the king, what you conceived in your heart was made known to me.

relationship: related attribution of strength and wealth
rationale: Ezekiel asks whether the ruler's knowledge and understanding produced his strength, gold and silver. Deuteronomy warns against claiming that one's own strength gained wealth and identifies God as the giver of that ability, preserving Ezekiel's question and Deuteronomy's explicit instruction.
source_text: Surely it was not by your knowledge or understanding that you built up strength for yourself, and gold and silver in your treasuries?

target_units.text: Do not say in your heart: My strength and the might of my hand have gotten me this great wealth.
And you shall remember the Lord your God, for He gives you strength to gain wealth, that He may establish His covenant which the Lord sware unto your fathers, as at this day.

relationship: parallel abundance associated with a lifted-up heart
rationale: The ruler's great knowledge and commerce increase his strength, and his heart is lifted up in that strength. Deuteronomy similarly warns that multiplied possessions, silver and gold may accompany a lifted-up heart and forgetting God; the target gives a warning rather than Tyre's reported condition.
source_text: By your abundant knowledge and your trade you increased your strength; your heart was exalted in your strength.

target_units.text: lest, when you have eaten and are filled, and have built good houses and dwelt in them,
and your herds and your flocks are multiplied, and your silver and your gold are multiplied, and all that you have is multiplied,
you become lifted up in heart, and forget the Lord your God, who brought you forth out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of bondage;

relationship: same-chapter repeated charge of a godlike heart
rationale: The announced judgment is grounded in the ruler's setting his heart like a god's heart. Verse 2 had already joined that charge to his divine claim and the correction that he is human, supplying the stated offense behind the response.
source_text: Therefore thus says the Lord: Since you made your heart like a god’s heart,

target_units.text: “And you, son of man, say to the ruler of Tyre: Thus says the Lord: Because your heart was exalted and you said, ‘I am a god; I have inhabited a god’s dwelling in the heart of the sea’—yet you are a human, and not a god, and you made your heart like a god’s heart—

relationship: same-chapter beauty and knowledge corrupted and judged
rationale: Foreigners strike the beauty of the ruler's knowledge and destroy his beauty. Verse 17 likewise joins beauty and knowledge, there explaining pride and corruption before the ruler is cast down as a spectacle, preserving the different means and explanation.
source_text: therefore, behold, I am bringing foreigners against you, scourges from nations. They will draw their swords against you and against the beauty of your knowledge, and lay your beauty out for destruction,

target_units.text: Your heart was exalted because of your beauty; your knowledge was corrupted together with your beauty. Because of your many sins I threw you to the ground; I placed you before kings to be made a spectacle.

relationship: related descent of Tyre and its ruler amid sea imagery
rationale: The ruler is brought down and dies a wounded person's death in the sea. The city oracle likewise combines covering waters with Tyre's descent among the ancient dead, using the city's pit imagery rather than explicitly naming a pit in this ruler's unit.
source_text: and they will bring you down; you will die the death of wounded men in the heart of the sea.

target_units.text: For thus says the Lord, the Lord: When I make you a desolated city like cities that will not be inhabited, when I bring the abyss up over you and much water covers you,

I will bring you down to those descending into the pit, to the people of old. I will settle you in the depths of the earth like an everlasting wilderness, with those descending into the pit, so that you are not inhabited and do not rise in the land of life.

relationship: related god-language confronted with human death
rationale: The ruler's claim to be a god is challenged before those killing him, since he is human. The psalm likewise places god-language beside dying like human beings, though there God addresses the group as gods rather than reporting a ruler's own boast.
source_text: Surely you will not say, ‘I am a god,’ before those killing you? You are a human, and not a god. In a multitude

target_units.text: “I said, ‘You are gods, and all sons of the Most High.’
But you die like human beings, and fall like one of the rulers.”

relationship: parallel royal death associated with the uncircumcised
rationale: The sentence concerning Tyre's ruler associates uncircumcised people with his perishing by foreign hands. The Egypt lament likewise assigns the addressee a place among the uncircumcised and those wounded by the sword, sharing the death description while differing in the named agent and royal setting.
source_text: of uncircumcised people you will perish by foreigners’ hands, for I have spoken, says the Lord.”

target_units.text: You too will lie among the uncircumcised with those wounded by the sword.

relationship: related beauty of Tyre's ruler and the city
rationale: The lament calls Tyre's ruler a seal of likeness and crown of beauty. The city portrait likewise repeats clothing with beauty, first in Tyre's own words and then by its sons, providing a related city motif without adding wisdom to the supplied royal description.
source_text: “Son of man, take up a lament over the ruler of Tyre and say to him: Thus says the Lord, the Lord: You were a seal of likeness and a crown of beauty;

target_units.text: and say to Tyre, who dwells at the entrance of the sea, the trading place of the peoples from many islands: Thus says the Lord to Tyre: You said, ‘I have clothed myself with my beauty.’
In the heart of the sea, at Beelim, your sons clothed you with beauty.

relationship: related divine garden and precious-material imagery
rationale: The ruler is described in God's paradise of delight with an extensive list of precious materials. Genesis describes God's garden in Eden and the associated river country containing gold and stones; the garden and materials correspond without identifying the ruler with Adam or equating the two lists.
source_text: you came to be in the delight of God’s paradise. You have been clothed with every good stone: carnelian, topaz, emerald, carbuncle, sapphire, jasper, silver, gold, ligurite, agate, amethyst, chrysolite, beryl, and onyx. You filled your treasuries and storehouses within you with gold from the day you were created.

target_units.text: And the Lord God planted a garden in Eden, toward the east, and there He placed the man whom He had formed.
And God caused every tree that was beautiful to behold and good for food to spring up from the earth, with the tree of life in the midst of the garden, and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.
And a river flows out of Eden to water the garden, and from there it divides into four branches.
The name of the first is Pishon; it flows around the whole land of Havilah, where there is gold.
And the gold of that land is good; there also are the carbuncle and the green stone.

relationship: overlapping precious stones in royal and priestly adornment
rationale: The ruler's stone list overlaps the oracle-piece's rows in such stones as emerald, sapphire, jasper and amethyst. Exodus assigns its stones to Israel's tribes and priestly clothing; Ezekiel's larger list and royal lament do not make the ruler that priest or reproduce the same arrangement.
source_text: you came to be in the delight of God’s paradise. You have been clothed with every good stone: carnelian, topaz, emerald, carbuncle, sapphire, jasper, silver, gold, ligurite, agate, amethyst, chrysolite, beryl, and onyx. You filled your treasuries and storehouses within you with gold from the day you were created.

target_units.text: You shall weave into it a fabric set with four rows of stones. The first row shall be a sardius, topaz, and emerald;
the second row a carbuncle, sapphire, and jasper;
the third row a ligure, agate, and amethyst;
the fourth row a chrysolite, beryl, and onyx. They shall be enclosed in gold and bound in gold according to their rows.
The stones shall bear the names of the sons of Israel, twelve according to their names, each engraved like a seal with the name of one of the twelve tribes.

relationship: related cherub presence in divine garden imagery
rationale: God places the ruler with the cherub on His holy mountain within the preceding paradise description. Genesis stations cherubim to guard the way to the tree of life; the shared imagery does not make Ezekiel's ruler himself the cherub.
source_text: With the cherub I placed you on God’s holy mountain; you came to be among fiery stones.

target_units.text: And He drove Adam out and settled him opposite the garden of delight. And He stationed the cherubim and the flaming sword that turns about, to guard the way to the tree of life.

relationship: related created uprightness and subsequent conduct
rationale: The ruler is blameless from his creation until wrongs are found in him. Ecclesiastes likewise states that God made humankind upright but people sought many reasonings, giving a broader human comparison without making the two passages describe the same person.
source_text: You were blameless in your days from the day you were created until wrongdoings were found in you.

target_units.text: Only behold, this I found: God made humankind upright, but they sought many reasonings.

relationship: related expulsion from privileged divine space amid cherub imagery
rationale: The ruler's lawlessness ends in removal from God's mountain, and the cherub leads him out from the fiery stones. Genesis likewise describes removal from the garden, but God drives Adam out and stations cherubim to guard the way; the agents and actions remain distinct.
source_text: From the abundance of your trade you filled your store chambers with lawlessness, and you sinned and were wounded away from God’s mountain; the cherub led you out from among fiery stones.

target_units.text: And the Lord God sent him out of the garden of delight to till the earth from which he had been taken.
And He drove Adam out and settled him opposite the garden of delight. And He stationed the cherubim and the flaming sword that turns about, to guard the way to the tree of life.

relationship: parallel proud royal elevation followed by a public fall
rationale: The ruler's heart is lifted up through beauty, his knowledge is corrupted, and he is thrown down before kings. Isaiah's Babylonian royal lament likewise moves from exalted ambitions to descent and astonishment among observers, without importing Ezekiel's beauty explanation into Isaiah or identifying either figure as Satan.
source_text: Your heart was exalted because of your beauty; your knowledge was corrupted together with your beauty. Because of your many sins I threw you to the ground; I placed you before kings to be made a spectacle.

target_units.text: How the dawn-bearer who rises in the morning fell from heaven! The one dispatching to all the nations was shattered to earth.
You said in your mind, ‘I will ascend to heaven, set my throne above heaven’s stars, and sit on a high mountain, upon the high mountains toward the north.
I will ascend above the clouds; I will be like the Most High.’
But now you will descend to Hades and to the earth’s foundations.
Those who see you will marvel at you and say, ‘Is this the person who provoked the earth, shook kings,

relationship: related lawlessness punished by burning and reduction to ashes
rationale: The ruler's injustices and unlawful trade lead to fire consuming him and ashes on the ground. Malachi likewise portrays practitioners of lawlessness burned and reduced to ashes underfoot; Ezekiel additionally specifies fire coming from within the ruler.
source_text: Because of your many sins and the wrongdoings of your trade you profaned your sacred places. I will bring fire out from within you; it will consume you. I will turn you to ashes on your land before all who see you.

target_units.text: For look, the day of the Lord is coming, burning like an oven, and it will burn them. All the foreigners and all who practice lawlessness will be straw, and the coming day will ignite them,” says the Lord Almighty, “and neither root nor branch will remain from them.
But for you who fear My name, a sun of righteousness will rise, and healing in its wings; you will go out and leap like little calves released from bonds.
You will trample the lawless, because they will be ashes beneath your feet on the day that I am making,” says the Lord Almighty.

relationship: repeated national dismay and permanent-ruin conclusion for Tyre
rationale: Those knowing the ruler among the nations become gloomy before the ruin-and-no-more declaration. The city lament likewise ends with gloomy island inhabitants and the same ruin conclusion, applying the repeated response to city and ruler respectively.
source_text: All who know you among the nations will become gloomy over you; you came to ruin, and you will no longer exist for ever.”

target_units.text: All who inhabit the islands became gloomy over you; their kings were utterly astonished, and their faces shed tears.
Traders from nations hissed at you; you came to ruin, and you will be no more for ever.’”

relationship: related divine address against Sidon
rationale: Ezekiel is told to face Sidon and prophesy against it. Joel likewise directly addresses Sidon alongside Tyre and promises recompense, there specifying the seizure of sacred valuables and sale of Judah's people rather than supplying those charges in Ezekiel's commission itself.
source_text: “Son of man, fix your face upon Sidon and prophesy against her,

target_units.text: What have you to do with Me, Tyre and Sidon and all Galilee of foreigners? Are you repaying Me a recompense? Or do you bear a sharp grudge against Me? I will speedily repay your recompense upon your heads,
because you took My silver and gold and brought My chosen and beautiful things into your temples,

rationale: God strengthens Babylon's king's arms and puts His sword in his hand. Isaiah likewise places the rod of God's anger and wrath in Assyrian hands; the weapon and empire differ, and the rod is not silently made identical with the Assyrians themselves.

target_units.text: Woe to the Assyrians! The rod of My anger and wrath is in their hands.

rationale: God strengthens the Babylonian king's arms and places His sword in that king's hand against Egypt, repeating the particular empowerment in verse 24. This unit additionally contrasts Pharaoh's falling arms, a detail not repeated in verse 24 itself.

target_units.text: I will strengthen the arms of the king of Babylon and put My sword into his hand; he will bring it upon Egypt, take her booty, and strip her spoils.

relationship: repeated Egyptian dispersion among nations and countries
rationale: The Egypt oracle closes with scattering among nations and dispersal into countries. Ezekiel 29 had announced the same displacement of Egyptians, joined there to forty-year desolation; this closing unit instead adds recognition of the Lord.

relationship: same-chapter repeated comparison framing Pharaoh's tree oracle
rationale: The address to Pharaoh and his multitude opens by asking whom he resembled in height. The closing unit repeats the question of likeness and expressly names Pharaoh and his strength, connecting the intervening tree portrait with its stated royal addressee.

relationship: parallel imperial tree reaching the clouds
rationale: Assyria is pictured as a beautiful, tall cypress whose crown reaches clouds. Daniel explicitly identifies the great tree with the king and interprets its heavenly height and cloud-reaching mass as royal elevation; Ezekiel names a cypress, while Daniel's tree has no species here.
source_text: Behold, Assyria was a cypress in Lebanon, beautiful in offshoots and tall in size; its crown reached into the midst of clouds.

target_units.text: You, O king, are the tree planted in the earth, whose appearance was great.
And all the birds of heaven nesting in it—the strength of the earth and of the nations and of all languages to the ends of the earth, and all countries—serve you.

The raising of that tree, its reaching heaven, and its mass touching the clouds mean that you, O king, were raised above all people upon the face of the whole earth. Your heart was raised in pride and strength against the Holy One and His angels. Your deeds were seen, because you laid waste the house of the living God on account of the sins of the consecrated people.

relationship: related tree growth sustained by abundant water
rationale: Water and the abyss nourish the imperial tree and its surrounding plantings. Jeremiah likewise compares the person trusting the Lord with a flourishing tree whose roots reach moisture, preserving the different represented subjects and the difference between this tree's eventual fall and Jeremiah's promise.
source_text: Water nourished it; the abyss raised it high, led its rivers around its plantings and sent out its gatherings of water to all the plain’s trees.

target_units.text: And blessed is the person who has trusted in the Lord, and the Lord will be his hope;

and he will be like a tree flourishing beside waters, and will send its roots toward moisture, and will not fear when heat comes. Wooded stems will be upon it; in a rainless year it will not fear or cease bearing fruit.

relationship: parallel exceptional height and spread of a great tree
rationale: The cypress rises above the other plain trees and spreads its branches because of abundant water. Daniel's tree likewise has immense height, cloud-reaching mass and exceptionally long branches, without giving Ezekiel's water explanation.
source_text: Therefore its size rose above all the plain’s trees, and its branches spread wide because of abundant water.

target_units.text: Its appearance was great: its top reached to heaven, and its mass to the clouds, filling what lay beneath heaven. The sun and moon dwelt in it and illuminated the whole earth.

Its branches were about thirty stadia long. All the wild animals of the earth found shade beneath it, and the birds of heaven nested in it. Its fruit was abundant and good, and it supplied all living creatures.

relationship: shared birds and beasts sheltered by an imperial tree
rationale: Birds nest in the cypress's offshoots, beasts give birth beneath its branches and nations inhabit its shade. Daniel's tree likewise shelters animals and nesting birds and supplies living creatures, without repeating Ezekiel's birth clause in that unit.
source_text: All the sky’s birds nested in its offshoots; all the plain’s beasts gave birth beneath its branches, and every multitude of nations lived in its shade.

target_units.text: Its branches were about thirty stadia long. All the wild animals of the earth found shade beneath it, and the birds of heaven nested in it. Its fruit was abundant and good, and it supplied all living creatures.

relationship: same-chapter beauty and growth attributed to plentiful water
rationale: The tree's beautiful height and many branches are explained by roots reaching abundant water. Verse 4 had described the waters and abyss nourishing it and supplying other trees, giving the particular source of growth developed here.

target_units.text: Water nourished it; the abyss raised it high, led its rivers around its plantings and sent out its gatherings of water to all the plain’s trees.

relationship: same-chapter unrivaled beauty followed by the other trees' envy

rationale: The earth is watered from the addressee's discharges and the ravines are filled with him. Verse 5 had laid his flesh on mountains and filled them with blood; the adjacent territorial body images correspond without replacing this unit's discharges with a repeated blood clause.

relationship: related companions falling with a defeated figure among sword-wounded people
rationale: Others fall with him among those wounded by the sword and all his strength lies down. The tree oracle similarly describes others descending with it to Hades among the sword-wounded, preserving the supplied pronouns rather than inventing an additional named companion.

rationale: Giants speak to the addressee in the pit and command descent among the sword-wounded. Isaiah likewise depicts underworld giants addressing the fallen Babylonian king and naming his shared captivity, with different words in the dead speakers' address.
